title: Simple Habits That Keep You Safe Online
script: Narrator: [warmly] A few months ago, a close friend of mine almost lost access to her email account completely.
Narrator: Someone had guessed her password, because it was simple, just her name and her birth year.
Narrator: [curious] That story scared me enough to finally fix my own online habits, which honestly were not much better.
Narrator: First, I stopped using the same password for every single account, which I had done for years.
Narrator: [honestly] It felt overwhelming at first, remembering different passwords for banking, email, and social media accounts.
Narrator: So I started using a password manager, an app that remembers strong passwords for me, safely.
Narrator: [carefully] Second, I turned on something called two-factor login, wherever it was available on my accounts.
Narrator: This adds another check, such as an authenticator app, security key, or one-time code.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Third, I became more careful about links in messages, especially ones asking me to click quickly, right now.
Narrator: If a message feels urgent or scary, that is usually exactly when I should slow down and check carefully.
Narrator: [practically] I also started checking who sent an email, not just the name shown, but the actual address itself.
Narrator: A legitimate service will not ask for my full password by email. I open its official app or website directly instead of using a message link.
Narrator: [reflective] None of these habits are complicated or expensive. They simply require a little attention and a little patience.
Narrator: My friend eventually got her account back, but it took weeks of frustrating phone calls and forms.
Narrator: [encouraging] I would rather spend ten minutes today than weeks later, trying to fix something that already went wrong.
Narrator: Online safety is not about fear. It is simply about a few small, steady habits.

quiz.question: What almost happened to the narrator's friend?
options: She almost lost access to her email account
quiz.explanation: The narrator's friend almost lost access to her email account because her password was easy to guess.

quiz.question: What was wrong with the friend's password?
options: It was simple, just her name and birth year
quiz.explanation: Someone guessed the password because it was simple, just her name and her birth year.

quiz.question: What did the narrator start using to manage passwords?
quiz.explanation: She started using a password manager, an app that remembers strong passwords for her safely.

quiz.question: What is two-factor login, according to the narrator?
options: Needing a code sent to your phone even if the password is guessed
quiz.explanation: She explains that even if someone guesses the password, they also need a code sent to her phone.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say about urgent-feeling messages?
options: They should always be clicked quickly
That is usually exactly when she should slow down and check carefully
quiz.explanation: She says if a message feels urgent or scary, that is when she should slow down and check carefully.

quiz.question: Why was the friend’s password weak?
options: It was stored in a manager
It had too many random words
It used a name and birth year
quiz.explanation: Personal details were easy to guess.

quiz.question: Why use different passwords?
options: One leak should not open every account
They are easier to post publicly
Companies ask for all of them

quiz.question: What may provide a second factor?
options: An authenticator, security key, or code
quiz.explanation: More than one safe method exists.

quiz.question: How should an urgent request be checked?
options: Open the official app or site directly
quiz.explanation: A separate official route avoids a fake link.

quiz.question: What will a legitimate service not request by email?
quiz.explanation: Passwords should never be sent through email.
